1150-the-danish-history-books-i-ix:
Saxo Grammaticus, a Danish clerk of about 1200, wrote the first nine books of his great history of Denmark, from legendary kings to the reign of Gorm the Old. Gods, heroes, and sea-kings crowd the tales, including Amleth, the prince whose story later became Hamlet.

Saxo writes in grand Latin prose, mixing myth with chronicle and praising Danish valor against foes. His work saved tales that would else be lost, and it shaped Denmark's sense of its past. This volume gives the mythic half of his history, in a plain English version.
1957-beatrix:
Camille Maupin, a woman writer, receives a letter one day and learns that the Marquise de Rochefide, her rival, may arrive tomorrow. The novel follows Camille Maupin, a woman writer, and Béatrix de Rochefide, the marquise whose arrival Camille announces with a letter received yesterday and a visit expected tomorrow.

The story turns on two women and the men between them, in Brittany and Paris, with Balzac's usual care for houses, clothes, and social rank. It is a novel of love and rivalry among artists and aristocrats. Its interest lies in Camille herself: a woman of talent watching a younger rival take the place she once held.
1968-the-human-comedy-introductions-and-:
Before the novels themselves come the maps: Balzac's prefaces and notes explaining how a whole society, from peasants to kings, was to be rendered in fiction. The introductions explain the plan: a whole society, from peasants to kings, rendered in fiction.

The appendix adds Balzac's political writing, handling the affairs of the world with boldness and industry if not invariably with wisdom. The later Revue Parisienne pieces show the same hand. The volume is essential reading for anyone tackling the Human Comedy, since it gives Balzac's own map of the territory he spent a lifetime charting.
2122-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle adds an appendix to his history of Frederick, opening with a piece translated years before the main work began. A Day with Friedrich, dated 23 July 1779, follows a head manager who was nephew to the poet Gleim. The appendix piece dates from the 1850s, before Carlyle had drafted the main history.

Carlyle's old commentary, written with the translation, is left in place, with only slight later additions. The appendix gives readers a close, late glimpse of the old king, and a note on how Carlyle built his great history. A day with the old king in 1779 gives readers Frederick in old age, plain and businesslike.
23599-the-big-fix:
George O. Smith wrote this tale of a horse race that had to be fixed, in a world where telepathy and psi powers, far from ending crime, only test human ingenuity. It is April, a couple of weeks before the Derby, and the narrator plays poker, a game of skill with nothing to do with the speed of horse flesh.

Phil Howland slips open and closes before the narrator can read his hand. The Greek stays impenetrable and blocks mind reading of the deck. Chicago Charlie's mind reads easy but cannot be trusted, as apt to think high to fool a foe as to think true. Smith spins the fix with wit and psi detail, as minds race faster than horses. Readers who like clever science fiction crime will enjoy the poker table prelude and the race that must, somehow, be bent to order.
26671-the-boy-crusaders-a-story-of-the-d:
J. G. Edgar, author of The Boy Princes, published this juvenile historical novel with Gall and Inglis at Edinburgh, with eight full-page illustrations. Edgar calls the Crusades armed pilgrimages, and singles out the expedition headed by Louis IX of France, with Joinville as its chronicler, as hardly less interesting than any other. His object is a faithful picture of Joinville's events and of the renowned French monarch.

Two striplings serve their chivalry apprenticeship at a feudal castle in northern England, take the cross, and embark for the East. They reach Cyprus, land at Damietta, and share the glory and disaster of the Christian army, including the carnage of Mansourah and the massacre of Minieh. Later chapters follow Joinville in peril, St. Louis in chains, a mission to Bagdad, and the end of the armed pilgrimage.
27086-the-dodge-club-or-italy-in-mdcccli:
James De Mille's The Dodge Club, or Italy in MDCCCLIX, published by Harper in 1872 with one hundred illustrations, follows a club of Americans through France and Italy in 1859. The chapters teach, in comic form, how to speak French, raise a crowd, quell a landlord, and travel without baggage.

From Paris and Orleans past the Rhone in rain to Marseilles, the club meets a retired organ-grinder, a philosophizing senator, and Dolores, an Italian maid learning English. A masquerade, a moonlight walk, and a landlord averaging 477 lies a day keep the farce rolling.
27696-a-fine-fix:
R. C. Noll's short science-fiction story opens with three jet-and-rotor craft landing in a farm field, where a farmer reports a light falling from the sky and the ground jumping. A general, a major, and two technicians set out to inspect the crater.

The tale plays on the theme named in its title: people pass responsibility along until someone questions their method, and then they bristle. Compact and wry, it blends a crashed-object mystery with a joke about how organizations handle blame. The craft settle in rolling dust beside a battered pickup truck driven out to meet them.
27922-david-and-the-phoenix:
Edward Ormondroyd wrote David and the Phoenix, illustrated by Joan Raysor and published in Chicago by Follett in 1957. The story begins when David, visiting a new house, looks up at a mountain and hears a mysterious voice, then meets the Phoenix itself.

Ten chapters follow David's education by the Phoenix, visits to gryffins, a sea monster, a banshee, and a faun, and a scientist in pursuit of the rare bird. The book ends with a five hundredth birthday celebrated in proper phoenix tradition, and it has become a beloved children's fantasy.
28252-violin-making-the-strad-library-no:
Walter H. Mayson wrote Violin Making, second edition, London, 1909, as number nine in The Strad Library, with thirty-one pictures. Mayson works through the whole craft in order: choice of wood, back, purfling, belly, soundholes, bass bar, ribs, scroll, neck, varnish, and fitting up. His preface jokes that prefaces feel like waiting for dinner after a winter walk.

Each chapter gives plain, practical steps for the bench, aimed at makers and repairers. Mayson stresses good wood, careful thickness, and clean work. The book remains a useful manual for violin makers and for readers who love fine craft.
28419-twenty-five-cent-dinners-for-famil:
Juliet Corson wrote Twenty-Five Cent Dinners for Families of Six, thirteenth edition, New York, 1879, as a cookery reform book. Corson, superintendent of the New York Cooking School, thanks press and public for success beyond her hopes. She adds a chapter on fresh fruit for dessert, against rich preserves and the national pie. Orange Judd Company published the volume.

Corson, author of Fifteen-Cent Dinners for Workingmen's Families, gives plain, cheap, healthy dinners for six, with costs counted. Her aim is culinary reform for working homes. The book offers a practical, humane record of American cooking on a tight budget.
28653-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Volume 9 of The Best of the World's Classics, subtitled America I, 1579 to 1891, was published by Funk and Wagnalls in 1909. Henry Cabot Lodge served as editor-in-chief, with Francis W. Halsey as associate editor, and each piece carries biographical and explanatory notes. The volume restricts itself to prose, sampling American writing across three centuries.

John Smith tells of Pocahontas, Bradford of Pilgrims meeting Indians, and Sewall of courting Madam Winthrop. Franklin, Washington, Adams, Paine, Jefferson, Morris, and Hamilton follow, with Channing closing the span. Readers get a compact anthology of American prose at its most quotable.
32231-among-the-wild-tribes-of-the-afgha:
T. L. Pennell's Among the Wild Tribes of the Afghan Frontier, a record of sixteen years' intercourse with the natives of the marches, was published in London by Seeley and Company in 1909. It is the second edition. It has an introduction by Field-Marshal Earl Roberts and thirty-seven illustrations and two maps. Pennell, a doctor and fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, dedicates the book to his mother. To her life and teaching he owes more than he can record.

Its first chapter, The Afghan Character, treats paradox, honour, blood-feuds, a sister's revenge, and an outlaw. It continues through a jirgah and its termination, bluff, and an attempted kidnapping. Hospitality, a midnight meal, an ungrateful patient, a robber's death, a dance and an officer's escape follow. A second chapter treats Afghan traditions: Israelitish origin, Jewish practices, shrines, burial customs, and charms. Readers get a doctor's memoir.
32427-category-phoenix:
Boyd Ellanby's tale, printed in Galaxy in May 1952, opens with Dr. David Wong hiding a notebook as an imperative knock sounds at his office door. Wong steps from behind a pivoting bookcase, presses a desk button to release the lock, and faces a black-uniformed Ruler and a watchguard. The Ruler rebukes him for a locked door, citing Leader Marley's maxim that constructive science does not skulk behind locked doors.

Wong's secret work touches a society where knowledge of extending life has become a passport to death. Ellanby sets a lone researcher against a regime that treats science as state property and privacy as guilt. The story turns on what a person will risk to keep knowledge alive when the state claims the right to own it.
3832-australia-felix:
Henry Handel Richardson opens her great Australian trilogy with a shaft accident on the Ballarat goldfields. A digger, buried alive when a drive collapses, dies with his ribs jammed across his pick and his mouth pressed into mud. His mates at the windlass haul up only bad news. Such accidents, Richardson notes, were not infrequent, and each man takes the risk in his stride.

The novel then follows Richard Mahony, an Irish doctor on the diggings, and his young wife Polly, whose homecoming after a journey fills the house with talk. Letters from home, a headdress of black pearls and frosted leaves, and talk of politics after a year of mourning mark the couple's slow rise. Readers who like colonial fiction will find a rich and somber start to a long story.
401-blix:
Frank Norris sets this San Francisco novel in 1899, among the Bessemer family on Washington Street hill. Blix, a bright young woman, meets the journalist Condy Rivers, and their talk, walks, and quarrels shape a slow courtship. Bay views, Sunday breakfasts, and city streets form the warm ground of their days.

Norris writes with a light, keen eye for manners, food, and young pride. Blix teases, scolds, and charms Condy into seeing life more plainly. The novel reads as a fresh, sunny romance of youth in a young city, before Norris turned to darker tales of greed and fate.
5699-the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint's science romance The Emancipatrix opens with a mental expedition, as a doctor and a geologist test strange powers of thought. The doctor closes a door, crosses to a table, and silently offers the geologist a first step into an experiment that will carry the story beyond ordinary adventure. Flint, writing in the pulp tradition, mixes scientific speculation with brisk, colorful action.

Readers follow minds at work as much as bodies in motion, since the novel treats thought itself as a force that can travel and change events. The tale suits fans of early science fiction who enjoy bold ideas stated plainly and pursued without apology. Its period charm lies in earnest wonder: new knowledge opens new dangers, and human will must learn to guide them.
5965-the-devolutionist-and-the-emancipat:
Homer Eon Flint opens in the private study of Dr. William Kinney, a room of books, surgical and psychological instruments, star charts, and maps. Mrs. Kinney leads a caller in with a warning not to make a sound, whatever he sees. Four chairs hold four human beings who sit absolutely motionless, chests barely rising.

The caller can hardly tell whether they breathe, and senses that the seated figures are connected in some strange way. Flint builds a science-fiction mystery from this single tableau of stillness and experiment. The tale asks what has been done to these minds, and what it may cost to wake them.
6338-boy-scouts-in-the-coal-caverns-or-t:
Give me a good husky band of Boy Scouts, says Case Canfield, caretaker of the Labyrinth mine, and they will do the job if it can be done. Four lads of seventeen in khaki, George Benton, Charley Sandy Green, Tommy Gregory, and Will Smith of the Beaver Patrol, Chicago, take up the challenge. Will is scoutmaster, George patrol leader, and their past books have carried them from Pictured Rocks to Everglades, continental caverns, and Hudson Bay snows.

Camping in the breaker opens this tale, and a light in tunnel six gives it its second title. A new saw, never used before, becomes a clue worthy of Sherlock Holmes, for the man who cut with it must have bought it at a nearby store. Major Fletcher writes a boys' adventure of mines, teamwork, and detection, where scouting skill meets a real underground puzzle.
8398-the-sign-at-six:
Stewart Edward White wrote this mystery novel around a sign at six. Its contents promise a strange brew: the owner of New York, a shadow of mystery, darkness and panic, and a scientist in pink silk. The wrath to come, a world of ghosts, Percy Darrow's theory, the great silence, and the lifting of the spell follow. The story moves from high society to hidden science.

White, known for western and adventure tales, tries here a tale of mystery and the uncanny in modern New York. Readers get a plot-driven novel with a scientific twist, in the style of early twentieth-century thrillers. The sign itself, whatever it proves to be, hangs over the action as a warning and a riddle.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-ix:
The ninth tome of Les Prairies d'Or, printed in 1877, completes Barbier de Meynard's French al-Masudi. The Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the Meadows of Gold, is the work of a tenth-century Baghdad scholar who traveled to India, Persia, and East Africa. With this tome the Société Asiatique set stands whole.

Al-Masudi aimed at nothing less than the whole known world. He covers its lands and seas, its ancient kings, and its faiths. The annals of Islam run down to his own time. His method mixes chronicle, geography, and the tales of the road. The French version remains the fullest form of his book in a Western tongue. The long labor of the editors ends here.
australia-felix:
Henry Handel Richardson, pen name of writer Ethel Robertson, opened her Richard Mahony story with Australia Felix on the Victorian goldfields. A proem buries a digger in a collapsed shaft on the Gravel Pits, while his mate Long Jim weeps for his luck. Richardson builds the novel from her father's life as a goldfields doctor. Fortune will smile and ruin by turns.

Richard Mahony, an English doctor, throws up medicine for digging and trade in Ballarat. Fever lifts and drops him as claims fail, flood, and pay out without pattern. Marriage to Mary Turnham brings steadiness he cannot keep, and pride wounds his chances. Stores, shares, and starts cycle through the town's boom years. Richardson writes the fields with mud, water, and failure in detail. Readers of classics start the Mahony trilogy here, where a man's hunger for fortune shows the flaw that dogs him through later volumes.
beatrix:
Honore de Balzac's Beatrix, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, carries a note admitting what Balzac usually escaped: readers recognized real persons in this novel. The Marquise de Rochefide, Beatrix, was drawn from Marie d'Agoult, and Camille Maupin, the woman writer in the tale, from George Sand. The Breton setting at Guerande frames their rivalry.

Calyste du Guenic, a noble Breton youth, loves Beatrix, who plays with his devotion while Camille, older and wiser, studies him and forgives much. A letter in the middle weighs whether women sure of being loved pardon a passing infidelity as a triumph. Balzac turns a society scandal into a study of youth, genius, and manipulation.
blix:
Frank Norris published Blix in 1899, a short San Francisco love story named for its heroine, Travis Bessemer, called Blix. She lives with her family in a flat on the Washington Street hill, above a famous view of the bay. Young writer Condy Rivers courts her through long talks, walks, and shared jokes.

Norris keeps the plot light: fishing trips, a Chinese restaurant, newspaper work, and Blix's blunt refusal to be merely decorative. She counts out her own savings to help Condy, and the two test whether affection can survive ambition and separation. The novel shows Norris's softer side, far from his later tales of wheat and greed, and preserves a vivid picture of 1890s San Francisco.
boy-scouts-in-the-coal-caverns-or-the-li:
Boy Scouts in the Coal Caverns, or The Light in Tunnel Six, is credited on its title page to Major Archibald Lee Fletcher. The story opens in the dusky office of the idle Labyrinth mine. Case Canfield, the caretaker, addresses four lads of seventeen in scout khaki. Give me a good husky band of Boy Scouts, he says. They will do the job if it can be done.

The four are the Beaver Patrol of Chicago. Will Smith is Scoutmaster and George Benton Patrol Leader. Sandy Green and Tommy Gregory complete the party. Their sleeve medals show examinations passed as ambulance aids, stalkers, pioneers, and seamen. A Chicago criminal lawyer has sent them to the deserted mine. Its veins have not given out, Canfield hints. Something else closed it. Fletcher's series sends scouts wherever danger keeps a secret, and a coal mine keeps several.
britannica-1911-albert-of-aix:
Albert of Aix wrote a twelve-book history of the First Crusade without ever seeing the Holy Land. He flourished near A.D. 1100, having been born late in the eleventh century, and served as canon and custos, or keeper, of the church at Aix-la-Chapelle. Nothing more is known of his life. The work itself, written between 1125 and 1150, made his name.

His Historia Hierosolymitanae expeditionis starts at the council of Clermont, tracks the crusade's course, and tells of the Latin kingdom of Jerusalem in its first years, breaking off sharply in 1121. William of Tyre leaned hard on the first six books. Scholars of later times once scorned the history's worth, but the soundest view holds it a broadly true account with some tales mixed in. Albert gained his facts by talking at length with crusaders home from the east and by reading their letters.
britannica-1911-bisectrix:
Bisectrix is a geometry and crystallography term, the feminine form of the Latin bisector, from bi-, two, and secare, to cut. In geometry it is the same as bisector in plain use. It may be a point that splits a line into two equal parts. It may also be a line that splits an angle into two equal parts. The 1911 Britannica entry gives both plain senses in two lines.

In crystallography the word takes a narrower sense. There it names the bisector of the angle between the optic axes of a crystal. Those axes guide how light behaves inside the stone. The entry is a short glossary note of a few lines. It gives the Latin build of the word, the two geometry senses, and the crystal sense. No figures or examples appear in the text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aix:
Aix, Aquae Sextiae, in full the Archdiocese of Aix, Arles, and Embrun, covers Aix and Arles districts in the Bouches-du-Rhone. Before the Revolution, Aix's archdiocese counted Apt, Riez, Frejus, Gap, and Sisteron as suffragans. Today Arles and Embrun no longer exist as archbishoprics, and Aix has Marseille, Frejus, Digne, Gap, Ajaccio, and Nice as dependents.

Tradition makes St. Maximinus, one of the seventy-two disciples and Mary Magdalen's companion, the first Bishop of Aix. Duchesne seems to have proved this saint was not Aix's first bishop, nor linked to Mary Magdalen except in recent legends devised about the mid-eleventh century by Vezelay monks. The first historically known bishop is Lazarus, about the beginning of the fifth century. Only late in the eighth century did Aix become an archbishopric, having depended until then on Arles. In 1905 the archdiocese had 188,872 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-crucifi:
The altar crucifix is the altar's principal ornament, set there to recall that the Victim offered on the altar matches the one on the Cross. It must stand on the altar whenever Mass is celebrated, at the middle between the candlesticks, large enough for celebrant and people to see conveniently. Benedict XIV's constitution Accepimus of 16 July 1746 fixed the requirement.

Two exceptions allow the regular crucifix to stay. One is when the Crucifixion itself is the altarpiece's principal part. The other is when the Blessed Sacrament is exposed, following local custom. A saint merely holding a crucifix in a picture does not count as the first case. From Passion Sunday's first Vespers to the Good Friday unveiling, the altar crucifix wears a violet veil, white on Holy Thursday and black permitted on Good Friday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archaeology-o:
The Archaeology of the Cross and Crucifix traces the sign of the cross from a primitive mark long predating Christianity to the Christian crucifix, the cross bearing Christ's body. In simplest form, two lines crossing at right angles, the sign appears in East and West from remote antiquity, and some have claimed ethnographic importance for its spread. Though pleasing as decoration, it was from the earliest times not mere ornament but a symbol with religious meaning.

Its primitive form seems to have been the gamma cross, better known by its Sanskrit name swastika. Later it was curved at the ends or enriched with lines and points meeting at the centre. From those early signs the long article follows the cross into Christian art, worship, and devotion, showing how a universal mark became the central emblem of a faith. It also shows how the bare cross grew into the crucifix.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beatrix:
Beatrix is a name borne by several holy women, none of very eminent renown. The Roman virgin and martyr Beatrix, inscribed on 29 July, is believed sister to martyrs Simplicius and Faustinus, whom she buried. Legend says her betrothed Lucretius denounced her as Christian, and her own servants strangled her. Beatrix d'Este, who died in 1262, lost her betrothed Galeazzo Manfredi to battle wounds just before their wedding.

Refusing to return home, she served God under the Benedictine rule at San Lazzaro outside Ferrara, her festival kept on 19 January. Another Beatrix, the Bohemian Bozena, became a nun and was honored on 13 November as St Hrosnata's sister. A later Beatrix, honored by Queen Isabel the Catholic, founded an order for the Immaculate Conception, approved in 1480, but died ten days before its inauguration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestin-jose:
Célestin Joseph Félix was a French Jesuit born at Neuville-sur-l'Escaut on 28 June 1810 and dying at Lille on 7 July 1891. After studies at Cambrai and a spell teaching rhetoric, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1837, studied at Louvain, and was ordained in 1842. His early Lenten sermons, above all one on true patriotism preached at Ath, won him a brilliant name for eloquence.

Called to Paris, he preached at St. Thomas d'Aquin, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Saint-Sulpice. From 1853 to 1870 he held the pulpit of Notre-Dame, succeeding Lacordaire and de Ravignan. Critics found him short on imagination and on Lacordaire's fire, but stronger in dialectic and surer in doctrine, with a richer diction than de Ravignan's and more originality than Monsabré's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-la:
Charles de la Croix was a missionary born at Hoorbeke-St-Corneille in Belgium in 1792 and dead at Ghent in 1869. At Ghent seminary he resisted Napoleon's imposed bishop with fellow students. He and his brother Joseph were jailed at Wesel, where Joseph died. After the Empire fell he resumed his studies. Ordained by Bishop Dubourg of Louisiana, he followed him to the United States with seminarians and Flemish workmen.

In May 1818 he was sent to Barrens, Missouri, to oversee a new seminary for the Louisiana diocese. That December he moved to Florissant, near St. Louis. Helped by the Religious of the Sacred Heart, he laboured among Catholic families and Osage Indians, preparing the way for De Smet's Jesuits in 1823. When Van Quickenborne arrived with eight Belgian companions, de la Croix had nearly finished and paid for a brick church. He returned to Belgium in 1833, a canon of Ghent cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-vic:
Eugene Delacroix truly founded the nineteenth-century French romantic school. Born near Paris in 1798, he studied at the school of Fine Arts under Guerin. His Dante and Virgil of 1822 shocked critics and won notoriety. The Massacre of Scio in 1824 renewed the critical storm.

Travel in Spain and Morocco in 1831 filled his later work with southern light and colour. Algerian Women and the Crusaders' Constantinople rank among his greatest masterworks. He entered the Institute of France in 1857 after a quarter century of struggle. His output reached some 9,140 works before his death in 1863.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-xavi:
Francois-Xavier Charlevoix, born at Saint-Quentin on 24 October 1682 and dead at La Fleche on 1 February 1761, was a Jesuit historian of New France. He entered the Society at sixteen in 1698, studied philosophy at Louis-le-Grand, then taught grammar at Quebec from 1705 to 1709, gathering material for his coming History of New France. Back in Paris he studied theology for four years, and in 1720 the French court sent him travelling through the French colonies to seek information for discovering the Western Sea.

Sailing from La Rochelle in July 1720, he reached Quebec, went up the St. Lawrence and through the Great Lakes to Michillimackinac, visited the Winnebago country, followed Lake Michigan's eastern shore to the Illinois, and descended the Mississippi to its mouth. Shipwreck near the Bahamas delayed him, but he returned by Florida, reached San Domingo in September 1722, and sailed for Havre that December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guadix:
Spain's Diocese of Guadix covers most of Granada province and part of Almería, on the site of Roman Acci among the Bastetani. Legend in the Mozarabic Missal makes St. Torquatus, one of the Seven Apostolic Men, its first bishop, and named bishops reappear at the councils of Toledo before the last pre-invasion name, Ricila, fades from record.

Through the Mozarabic period the see survived. Almohad destruction in the twelfth century ended it until Cardinal Mendoza restored it on 21 May 1492, joining Baza to it the next year. A cathedral begun in 1710 on the old mosque site, a seminary from 1595, and present figures of about 116,000 Catholics in 62 parishes complete the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-ix:
Pope Leo IX (1049-1054) was born Bruno at Egisheim, near Colmar on Alsace's borders, on 21 June 1002. He came from a noble family that had given the Church saints and the Empire rulers. At five he was put under Berthold, Bishop of Toul, who ran a school for sons of the nobility. As a youth he survived a grave injury from an animal attack while at home on holiday.

Bruno became a St. Stephen's canon at Toul in 1017 and won a name for steadying others, including the choleric successor of Bishop Berthold. Sent to the court of his cousin Conrad in 1024 to serve in the royal chapel, he was known there as the good Bruno. In 1026, still a deacon, he led the Toul contingent into Italy when the aged bishop could not, a soldier's task that seems to have suited him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marie-dominiq:
Dominique Bouix was one of the best known modern French canonists, born at Bagneres-de-Bigorre in 1808 and dead at Montech in 1870. In 1825 he entered the Jesuits at Avignon with his brother Marcel, teaching classics, philosophy, and theology in order houses. In 1842, on the verge of solemn profession, poor health forced him to leave the society, a bitter disappointment softened by lifelong friendship with his former brethren.

A fifth Univers article restating canon law on synods cost him his chaplaincy and set his life's course: clearing French clergy of errors on law and discipline. Four years of study at Rome from 1851 to 1855, a doctorate in both laws in 1854, and treatise after treatise built his fame. He founded the Revue des sciences ecclesiastiques at Arras in 1860, became vicar-general of Versailles in 1864, and attended the Vatican Council as theologian to Montauban's bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minucius-feli:
Minucius Felix, a Christian writer who lived between 160 and 300, is known for his Octavius. His exact date is not known. That talk shows many points of likeness with Tertullian's Apologeticum, once put down to a lost Latin work both men used. This guess is now set aside, since so full a loss seems not likely.

Lactantius, who lists the writers before him, shows no hint of such a work. The Octavius sets a talk between the Christian Octavius and the pagan Caecilius, as they walk the shore at Ostia. It defends the faith from charges of godlessness, vice, and treason, with grace and skill. It stands as one of the best Latin defences of the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-raffei:
Pierre Raffeix was a French Jesuit missionary and mapmaker in seventeenth-century Canada. He was born at Clermont in 1633 and joined the order in 1653. He reached Canada ten years later. In 1668 he founded near Montreal a settlement for converted Iroquois that survives as Caughnawaga.

He then served the Cayuga and Seneca missions until 1680, sharing the dangers of the Iroquois frontier. Later he acted as procurator, or business manager, of the mission from Quebec. His surviving maps of western Canada, Lake Ontario, and New France, still kept in Paris, mark him as a learned cartographer as well as a missionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict IX, nephew of his two immediate predecessors, was a disgrace to the Chair of Peter. His father Alberic, treating the papacy as an heirloom, placed him on it as a youth, apparently about twenty in October 1032. Little is known of his pontifical acts, except that he held two or three synods in Rome and granted privileges to churches and monasteries. He insisted that Bretislav, Duke of Bohemia, found a monastery for carrying off Saint Adalbert's body from Poland.

In 1037 he went north to meet Emperor Conrad and excommunicated Heribert, Archbishop of Milan. Taking advantage of his dissolute life, a city faction drove him out in 1044 and elected the antipope Sylvester III. Benedict expelled Sylvester the same year, but resigned to Archpriest John Gratian for a large sum, making Gregory VI pope in May 1045. Repenting, he tried to depose Gregory, and all three claimants were deposed at Sutri in 1046.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-boniface:
Pope Boniface IX, born Piero Tomacelli of an ancient but impoverished Neapolitan baronial family, was elected at Rome on 2 November 1389 and died there on 1 October 1404. He lacked theological training and curial skill but was tactful and prudent by nature. His firm character and mild manner restored respect for the papacy across Germany, England, Hungary, Poland, and most of Italy.

As successor of the Roman pope Urban VI against the Avignon pope Clement VII, he crowned the young Ladislaus king of Naples at Gaeta in May 1390. He spent a decade expelling Angevin forces from Italy. He extinguished Rome's municipal independence and fortified Sant'Angelo and the bridges. He regained the Papal States' strongholds and steadfastly refused to abdicate, even when England, the Diet of Frankfurt, and King Wenceslaus urged it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement IX, born Giulio Rospigliosi at Pistoia on 28 January 1600, was elected on 20 June 1667 and died at Rome on 9 December 1669. He studied brilliantly at the Roman Seminary and Pisa, taking his doctorate at twenty-three and becoming professor of philosophy. Urban VIII, a fellow lover of letters, favoured him and sent him as nuncio to Spain.

In retirement under Innocent X, who disliked the Barberini circle, he returned under Alexander VII as secretary of state and cardinal in 1657. Elected unanimously a month after Alexander's death, he became the Romans' idol less for erudition than for charity and affability. He bought off the grain monopolist and heard confessions in Saint Peter's twice a week. He visited hospitals and gave lavishly to the poor. He refused to enrich his family or put his name on his buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory IX, born Ugolino, Count of Segni, about 1145 at Anagni, died on 22 August 1241 at Rome. Educated at Paris and Bologna, Innocent III, his uncle, named him papal chaplain, Archpriest of Saint Peter's, and Saint Eustachio's Cardinal-Deacon in 1198. Ostia and Velletri's Cardinal-Bishop he became in May 1206.

The next year brought him and Cardinal Brancaleone to Germany as legates, mediating between Philip of Swabia and Otto of Brunswick, rival claimants to the German throne after Henry VI's death. They freed Philip from the ban incurred under Celestine III for invading the Pontifical States. Unable to make Otto give up his claims, they still effected a truce and returned to Rome in 1208. Honorius III charged Ugolino in January 1217 as plenipotentiary legate for Lombardy and Tuscia, to preach the crusade there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent IX, born Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti at Bologna on 22 July 1519, was elected on 29 October 1591 and died at Rome on 30 December 1591. His pontificate lasted only two months. After law studies and a doctorate in 1544, he served Cardinals Ardinghelli and Farnese, managing Farnese's Avignon archdiocese and Parma affairs. Named Bishop of Nicastro in 1560, he attended Trent in 1562.

Sent as nuncio to Venice by Pius V in 1566, he furthered the alliance of pope, Venice, and Spain against the Turks that won Lepanto in 1571. Returning to his diocese in 1572, resigning it, and moving to Rome, he became Patriarch of Jerusalem in 1575 and cardinal in December 1583, called the Cardinal of Santiquattro. During Gregory XIV's sickly reign the administration rested on him. The Spanish party raised him to the chair, where he backed Philip II and the League against Henry IV. He planned a reserve fund against extraordinary expenses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-ix:
Pope John IX, from Tivoli, son of Rampoald, rose early in 898 and died early in 900. Election and death dates alike stay uncertain. A Benedictine, he took priest's orders from Pope Formosus. Factions then filled Rome, and one tried to thrust its man Sergius, later Sergius III, onto the throne instead of John.

The ducal House of Spoleto perhaps favoured him, so John kept his place while Sergius suffered exile from the city and excommunication. Clever and moderate, John gathered several synods at Rome and elsewhere in 898 to curb faction violence. They damned Stephen VI's ghastly synod and burned its Acts. Re-ordinations came under ban, clergy degraded by Stephen regained their rank, and plunder of dead bishops' and popes' palaces faced suppression by church and state alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xvi:
Pope John XVIII, successor of John XVII, was consecrated at Christmas 1003 and died in June 1009. A Roman priest called Leo fathered him; Phasianus was his name before elevation. Crescentius's influence raised him too. Almost nothing survives of his pontificate beyond church administration.

He upheld the holdings and rights of several churches and convents, approved gifts to religious houses, and granted rights to Merseburg's restored see. The Roman Synod of June 1007 won his consent for Bamberg's see, which King Henry II had founded and endowed. Meingaudus of Trier and Elphege of Canterbury received the pallium from him. He fought hard against Sens's Archbishop Letericus and Fulco, Bishop of Orléans. They barred Fleury's Abbot Goslin from Rome's privileges and pressed him to burn the papal charters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-ix:
Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti was born at Sinigaglia in 1792. Refused a place in the pope's Noble Guard because of epileptic fits, he studied theology and was ordained in 1819. Pius VII sent him to Chile as auditor in 1823. Leo XII made him archbishop of Spoleto in 1827. There he talked four thousand fleeing revolutionaries into laying down their arms in 1831. Gregory XVI moved him to Imola and made him cardinal in 1840.

He was pope from 1846 to 1878, a reign filled with trials. Piedmont set aside its concordat, ended tithes, laicized schools, seized church property, and jailed or banished opposing bishops. His protests in 1850, 1852, 1853, and 1855 came to nothing. Concordats with Württemberg and Baden were revoked before they took hold. Prussia and other German states turned hostile too. The entry follows the long loss of his temporal power to his death at Rome in February 1878.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Stephen reigned from 939 to 942, becoming pope about 14 July 939 and dying about the end of October 942. His reign lasted a little over three years. Despite late writers' contrary claims, he was certainly a Roman holding SS Silvester and Martin's cardinal-priesthood. He backed the fading Carolingian dynasty, forcing nobles by threat of excommunication to stay loyal to Louis IV d'Outre-Mer, the Frankish king.

Throughout his reign he stood subject to Alberic, Prince of the Romans, leaving him little room to distinguish himself. Alberic's dominance meant Stephen could do little on his own account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-ix:
Louis IX, king of France from 1226 to 1270, came to the throne at eleven under his mother Blanche's strong regency. Born at Poissy on 25 April 1215 to Louis VIII and Blanche of Castile, he married Marguerite of Provence at nineteen and fathered eleven children. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death near Tunis to 25 August 1270.

Blanche's regency, 1226 to 1234, saw the Crown beat Raymond VII in Languedoc, Pierre Mauclerc in Brittany, and Philip Hurepel in the Ile de France. Fighting against Henry III of England stayed indecisive. Frangipani, whom Honorius III had sent as legate to Louis VIII in 1225, won Gregory IX from Henry's side. He secured tithes from diocesan chapters for Blanche's southern crusade, and received Raymond's submission at Paris before Notre-Dame. That submission ended the Albigensian war and prepared the south's union to France by Paris's treaty of April 1229.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-nabor-and: Nabor and Felix were martyrs of the Diocletian persecution in 303. Their relics rest at Milan, where a church stands over their tomb, and Ambrose himself praised their virtues. Later Acts about them have no historical value, since they merely copy the Acts of other martyrs. Those legends make them soldiers under Maximian, condemned at Milan and beheaded at Lodi, and their feast falls on 12 July.
doe-osti-3022112-report-on-inventory-of-: BOR-60 got inventory-reported, and this DOE text counts six capsule samples. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The capsules were six. The data were nuclear. The BOR-60 was samples. The capsules were inventory. The six were report.
doe-osti-3066504-demonstration-of-grid-s: Wheatridge got grid-services-demonstrated, and this DOE text mixes forming and following. The pages detail the renewable findings. The grid folks get their data. The technologies were grid. The data were grid. The following were grid. The renewable were findings.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-appen:
Thomas Carlyle's appendix to his Friedrich history prints a piece translated sixteen years earlier, some years before any part of the history itself was written, as his headnote explains. The intercalated commentary dates from the same early time and is now partly superfluous to diligent readers, he admits, but he leaves it where not compelled to change. The piece preserves his first approach to the Prussian materials.

Its dialogue scenes bring General von Ziethen, the rugged, brave old cavalryman with hanging brows and dim-fiery pious thoughts, before the king in direct speech. Readers of the whole twenty-one volumes can watch Carlyle's manner forming here: the documents quoted, hectored, and loved into narrative. The appendix is a workshop door left open.
the-danish-history-books-i-ix: Saxo Grammaticus, called Saxo the Learned, wrote his Danish History in Latin in the early years of the thirteenth century, as Douglas B. Killings's preparer's note explains. The English text rests on The Nine Books of the Danish History of Saxo Grammaticus, translated by Oliver Elton for the Norroena Society in 1905. Saxo wrote sixteen books in all, but Elton rendered only the first nine, and no public-domain English version of books ten through sixteen is known to the preparer. Only this note and a bibliography are present here.
the-devolutionist-and-the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint pairs two tales in The Devolutionist and The Emancipatrix. The first opens under the head Out of Their Minds. Mrs. Kinney leads a caller to a locked door with a warning: make no sound, no matter what he sees. She turns the key, and the two step softly into the private study of her husband, Dr. William Kinney.

The room itself is ordinary enough, with book shelves, cases of surgical and psychological instruments, star charts, maps, and astronomical apparatus. Its four chairs are not. Each holds a human being, and none of the four stirs as the pair enters. The doctor sits half reclined, gray head resting wearily on one shoulder. Mrs. Kinney whispers the names: Mr. Smith beside him, and opposite, Mr. and Mrs. Van Emmon, all sunk in complete, motionless sleep.
the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint's The Emancipatrix opens in a doctor's room, where a blunt question lands: what has come between the geologist Van Emmon and his wife? Van, calm but held tight, traces it to a joint probe of Capellette two months past. Both he and Billie still trust the Venusian formula, he says, and long to visit more worlds by telepathy.

Four friends can project their minds to other planets. What they find there tests their bonds on Earth. Flint, an early pulp hand, blends space travel with close talk of marriage and trust.
the-executor-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magaz:
Mrs. Oliphant's tale The Executor ran in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume eighty-nine, covering January to June 1861. The volume's title page names William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and their London house in Paternoster Row. The tale opens mid-scene: John Brown declares the woman was certainly mad, a strange speech for the place.

A grim parlour holds two decanters on a bare, shining table, blinds drawn, and half a dozen folk in mourning, their faces a mix of shock and spite. A will has just been read. Oliphant spins greed and duty from that charged room.
the-human-comedy-introductions-and-appen:
Honoré de Balzac's fiction project receives its frame in this volume. It gathers the introductions and appendix for The Human Comedy. George Saintsbury supplied an introduction and a brief biography. The appendix lists Balzac's titles in French. English translations stand beside them, grouped by his classifications. Balzac's own introduction of 1842 is reprinted. Saintsbury opens with a letter to Balzac's sister. Without genius, Balzac wrote, he was done for.

Saintsbury argues those words unlock the man. Libraries have been written about Balzac since. Few phrases sum him up so well. He had staked everything on an unproved gift. The volume suits readers moving through the novels in order. It also suits anyone who wants the author's own map. His fictional universe sorts into scenes of private, provincial, and Parisian life. Balzac invented that scheme himself.
the-sign-at-six:
Stewart Edward White's The Sign at Six carries four illustrations by M. Leone Bracker. Its contents list twenty-four chapters. The owner of New York opens the book. The shadow of mystery and the moving finger follow. Darkness and panic come at chapter four. Later headings promise a world of ghosts and the great silence. The lifting of the spell and the plague of cold also appear.

Chapter one introduces Percy Darrow in a single unfolding sentence. He is a young man of scientific training, White writes. His manners are indolent and his appearance effeminate. Hidden energy and absolute courage complete the portrait, the sentence says. There the portion shown breaks off, leaving Darrow lounging at the threshold of the mystery.
